# Volume 2 — IX A Question of Color

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

“That old bother Agatha Sowerby dropped by once more today, nagging me to contribute money for purchasing a vestry room carpet,” Mr. Pettifer declared angrily. “My hatred for that woman exceeds my feelings for anyone else I am acquainted with. In merely six words, she is capable of compressing an entire sermon—complete with text, commentary, and application—and launching it at your head as if it were a brick.”
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0000 }

Seated upon the border of the veranda, Nell—who was taking pleasure in the delight of a gentle west breeze sweeping over a recently tilled field during a dim November dusk and whistling an unusual short tune amid the gnarled fir trees beneath the garden—gazed back over her shoulder with her imaginative face.
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0001 }

“The problem stems from you and Mrs. Sowerby not comprehending each other,” she clarified. “Whenever individuals dislike one another, that is invariably the issue. My own initial feelings toward Mrs. Sowerby were not warm; however, learning to appreciate her happened as soon as I grew to comprehend her.”
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0002 }

“Mrs. Sowerby might be a taste that certain people acquire; however, I stopped eating bananas rather than continuing just because I was informed that I would eventually come to enjoy them,” Mr. Pettifer growled. “Furthermore, regarding the matter of comprehending her, I comprehend that she is an inveterate meddler, and I informed her of that fact.”
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0003 }

“Oh, that surely injured her feelings terribly,” Nell stated with reproach. “In what way could you utter a statement like that? A long time ago, I spoke a few terrible words to Mrs. Sowerby, yet it occurred while I was out of temper. Expressing them intentionally is something I could not do.”
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0004 }

“That was what actually happened, and my policy is to speak truthfully to everyone.”
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0005 }

“However, you fail to speak the entire truth,” Nell protested. “The unpleasant portion of the truth is all that you reveal. Indeed, you have informed me twelve times that red was the color of my hair, yet you have not a single time mentioned to me that my nose was pleasant.”
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0006 }

“I imagine you are aware of it without being told,” laughed Mr. Pettifer.
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0007 }

“I am aware that my hair is red as well . . . even though its shade is far deeper than before . . . which means there is no reason to inform me of that as well.”
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0008 }

“Alright, alright, I will attempt to refrain from bringing it up any further if it bothers you so much. You will have to forgive me, Nell. I am accustomed to speaking my mind, so people simply have to tolerate it.”
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0009 }

“Yet they are unable to prevent themselves from caring about it. Nor do I believe that your custom makes it any easier. How would you view someone who walked around poking pins and needles into individuals while declaring, ‘Pardon me, you shouldn't care about it . . . it is merely a habit of mine.’ Wouldn't you consider him insane? Furthermore, regarding Mrs. Sowerby being meddlesome, maybe she indeed is. However, did you inform her that she possessed a most compassionate heart and constantly aided the needy, and never uttered a single word when Timothy Cotton took a crock of butter from her dairy and informed his wife that he had purchased it from her? The next time they encountered each other, Mrs. Cotton reproached her with the fact that it had a turnip flavor, and Mrs. Sowerby merely stated she was regretful it had proved to be so inferior.”
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0010 }

“I imagine there are a few decent traits to her,” Mr. Pettifer admitted reluctantly. “That goes for the majority of people. Even I possess a few, despite how unlikely it may seem to you. Regardless, not a single cent from me will go toward that carpet. It feels like people in this place never stop asking for hand-outs. What is the status of your plan to paint the hall?”
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0011 }

“Excellently. A gathering of the B.V.I.S. took place last Friday evening, during which we discovered that sufficient funds had been pledged not only to paint the hall but also to put new shingles on the roof. The majority of folk contributed most generously, Mr. Pettifer.”
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0012 }

Nell possessed a sweet soul, yet she had the ability to infuse innocent italics with a degree of venom whenever the situation demanded it.
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0013 }

“Which hue will you choose for it?”
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0014 }

“A very pretty green is what we have chosen. Dark red will be used for the roof, naturally. The paint is being fetched from town by Mr. Roger Tulk today.”
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0015 }

“Which person secured the position?”
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0016 }

“Delford’s Mr. Joshua Tulk. The shingling is almost completed by him. The contract had to be awarded to him by us, because all of the Tulks . . . and four families exist, as you are aware . . . declared that not a single cent would be contributed by them if Joshua failed to secure it. A total of twelve dollars had been pledged among them and losing that seemed unwise to us, even though a few folks believe the Tulks shouldn’t have been yielded to by us. It is claimed by Mrs. Sowerby that they attempt to control all things.”
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0017 }

“The primary issue is whether this Joshua performs his duties effectively. Provided he succeeds, his name being Tulk or Pudding seems irrelevant to me.”
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0018 }

“They consider him a skilled worker, although he is reported to be quite an odd individual. He almost never speaks.”
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0019 }

“He’s certainly odd enough,” Mr. Pettifer remarked drily. “At any rate, that’s what the locals will label him. Talking was never really my thing until I arrived in Brierley, where I was forced to start simply to protect myself, otherwise Mrs. Sowerby would have claimed I was mute and launched a fund to get me instructed in sign language. Nell, you aren’t leaving already?”
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0020 }

“I must. This evening I have a bit of sewing to complete for Lucy. On top of that, Robin is likely breaking Thirza’s heart with a new piece of mischief by now. Early today his very first words were, ‘Where does the dark go, Nell? I want to know.’ My answer to him was that it traveled to the opposite side of the earth, yet following breakfast he announced that it did not . . . that it descended into the well. According to Thirza, she found him leaning over the well-box four separate times today, attempting to reach down into the dark.”
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0021 }

“He’s a rascal,” stated Mr. Pettifer. “Prior to my arrival from the barn yesterday, he had come over and plucked half a dozen feathers from the tail of Nutmeg. Ever since then, the poor bird has been drooping. You folks must have a great deal of trouble with those children.”
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0022 }

“Whatever is value-worthy requires a certain degree of effort,” Nell uttered, inwardly deciding to pardon the subsequent misdeed of Robin, regardless of what it could prove to be, because he had taken revenge on Nutmeg for her sake.
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0023 }

That evening, the hall paint was brought home by Mr. Roger Tulk, and the following day, painting was commenced by Mr. Joshua Tulk, who was a taciturn, surly man. Nobody interrupted him while he worked. “The lower road” was the name given to the location of the hall. Because this route was constantly wet and muddy during late autumn, travelers headed to Delford took the “upper” route, which was longer. Fir woods enclosed the hall so tightly that it could not be seen except from close by. In this isolation and self-reliance, which his unsociable nature cherished greatly, Mr. Joshua Tulk kept painting.
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0024 }

On Friday afternoon, having completed his task, he traveled back to his home in Delford. Not long after he left, Mrs. Agatha Sowerby came driving past, having risked the muddy lower road because she was curious about how the hall appeared with its fresh coat of paint. As she came around the spruce curve, the sight met her eyes.
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0025 }

Mrs. Sowerby was strangely moved by what she saw. Releasing the reins, she raised both hands and exclaimed “Gracious Providence!” Her gaze remained fixed as though her vision was deceiving her. After that, her laughter turned nearly hysterical.
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0026 }

“A mistake has surely occurred . . . it must have. I was certain those Tulks would ruin everything.”
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0027 }

Traveling back to her house, Mrs. Sowerby encountered numerous individuals along the route and paused to inform them regarding the hall. The intelligence spread with immense speed. While studying a text book in his residence, Hugh Carrow was told by his father’s hired boy at sunset, whereupon he hurried out of breath to Grey Shutters, with Gideon Duckett joining him along the journey. Beneath the large leafless willows at the yard gate of Grey Shutters, they encountered Isolde Pembroke, Odette Pullen, and Nell Harcourt, who were the very embodiment of despair.
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0028 }

“Hugh cried out, “Is it really not true, Nell?””
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0029 }

“That’s correct,” replied Nell, appearing like the tragedy muse. “Mrs. Sowerby dropped by while traveling from Delford to inform me. Oh, it is just terrible! What point is there in attempting to make anything better?”
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0030 }

“What is terrible?” inquired Oliver Mott, who came up right then carrying a bandbox from town that he had retrieved for Thirza.
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0031 }

“Have you not heard?” Odette asked in anger. “Well, the situation is merely this. . . Joshua Tulk went ahead and chose blue paint for the hall rather than green . . . an intense, vivid blue, the very tint employed for coloring carts and wheelbarrows. And Mrs. Sowerby claims that, particularly when paired with a red roof, it is the most unsightly hue for a structure that she has ever witnessed or pictured. A feather could literally have floored me upon hearing the news. Following all the difficulty we have experienced, it is tragic.”
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0032 }

“In what imaginable way could an error like that have occurred?” cried Isolde.
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0033 }

This merciless catastrophe was ultimately attributed to the Tulks. Morton-Harris paints had been selected by the Improvers, with the Morton-Harris paint tins being assigned digits corresponding to a color chart. A customer picked a preferred tone from the chart and made an order using the corresponding digit. The requested hue of green was Number 147, and after Mr. Roger Tulk conveyed a message to the Improvers through his son, John Andrew, stating that he intended to travel to town and would purchase their paint, the Improvers instructed John Andrew to inform his father to obtain 147. John Andrew forever maintained that this was what he communicated, yet Mr. Roger Tulk asserted just as firmly that John Andrew had specified 157; and that is where the issue remains currently.
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0034 }

Every home in Brierley that housed an Improver was filled with total consternation during that evening. The melancholy present at Grey Shutters was so profound that it subdued even Robin. Unable to be consoled, Nell cried.
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0035 }

“Even if my seventeenth birthday is nearly here, Thirza, I cannot help weeping,” she wept. “This is extremely humiliating. Furthermore, it signals the absolute demise of our social circle. People will just mock us until we cease to exist.”
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0036 }

In reality, much like in dreams, matters frequently turn out in reverse. The residents of Brierley failed to find it amusing; their fury was too great. Because their funds had paid for painting the hall, the error left them feeling deeply wronged. The community directed its wrath toward the Tulks. Responsibility for the blunder lay between Roger Tulk and John Andrew; furthermore, Joshua Tulk had to be a natural idiot to not realize something was amiss upon opening the containers and beholding the paint's hue. When subjected to this criticism, Joshua Tulk countered that Brierley’s preferred shades were not his concern, regardless of his personal views; his employment was to paint the structure, rather than discuss it; and he intended to collect his payment for doing so.
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0037 }

It was with a bitter spirit that the Improvers handed over his payment, having first sought the advice of Mr. Peter Mott, a magistrate.
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0038 }

Peter informed him, “That bill will need to be settled by you.” He added, “Because his statement is that no one ever specified the intended color, but rather he was simply handed the paint and instructed to proceed, he cannot be blamed for the error. Still, it is a terrible disgrace, and without a doubt, that hallway appears terrible.”
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0039 }

The unfortunate Improvers anticipated that Brierley would hold a stronger bias against them than before; nevertheless, the sentiment of the public shifted in their direction. It was believed that the keen, passionate small group who had labored so diligently toward their goal had received unfair treatment. Mrs. Sowerby advised them to persevere and demonstrate to the Tulks that there actually existed individuals in the world capable of accomplishing tasks without creating a mess. Mr. Major Tranter dispatched a message informing them that he would remove every stump alongside his farm's road frontage and sow it with grass at his personal cost; furthermore, Mrs. Hiram Mott visited the school on a certain day and secretly motioned Nell out to the porch to inform her that should the “Sassiety” wish to plant a bed of geraniums at the crossroads when spring arrived, they had no reason to fear her cow, as she would ensure the destructive beast was confined to secure limits. Even Mr. Pettifer, if he laughed inwardly at all, did so in secret, displaying nothing but empathy on the surface.
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0040 }

“Don’t worry about it, Nell. Although a majority of paints grow more hideous as time passes, that blue has already reached maximum ugliness, meaning its fading process can only make it look better. Furthermore, the shingle roof has been properly painted. From now on, people sitting in the hall won't get rained on. Regardless, you have achieved a great deal.”
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0041 }

“Yet from now on, Brierley’s blue hall is going to be a proverb across every adjacent settlement,” Nell remarked with bitterness.
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0042 }

And it must be acknowledged that it was indeed so.
{: #nw-v02-c09-p0043 }
